claims.text: The initial nanoparticles are equiatomic Co–Ni–Cu–Fe–Cr.
The initial nanoparticles are crystallized as a homogeneous solid solution.
High configurational entropy initially maintains structural homogeneity in these nanoparticles.
Above an unspecified temperature threshold within 473–1923 K, differences in pairwise elemental interactions promote atomic segregation.
Segregation above the threshold is concentrated at nanoparticle surfaces and grain boundaries.
Reducing conditions favor segregation relative to inert conditions.
At moderate temperatures, entropy of mixing stabilizes the single-phase solid solution.
At higher temperatures, differences in elemental pairwise interaction enthalpies cause selective segregation.
Cu preferentially segregates to nanoparticle surfaces.
A reducing atmosphere enhances atomic mobility in the nanoparticles.
A reducing atmosphere alters surface chemistry in a way that facilitates demixing.
Under inert conditions, the nanoparticles remain a stable, single-phase solid solution across the tested range.
Under inert conditions, lattice-parameter shifts are minimal.
Under reducing conditions, segregation produces detectable lattice-parameter shifts relative to the initial state.
Under reducing conditions, secondary phases emerge at nanoparticle surfaces.
Under reducing conditions, grain-boundary compositional profiles change relative to the initial state.
The onset temperature for segregation varies with nanoparticle size.
The onset temperature for segregation varies with local composition heterogeneity.
Rapid transient segregation or extremely subtle compositional changes may evade the selected in situ measurements.
The absence of statistically significant atmosphere-dependent structural or chemical differences throughout 473–1923 K would falsify the proposed reducing-atmosphere destabilization.
